body:
From Claude: `perf/benchmark_ratchet.jl` exists and is wired into CI, but it is armed on hardware it does not run on, so it has never compared anything.

The step lives in `.buildkite/pipeline.yml`, which runs `queue: central`. Baselines are keyed by GPU (`perf/benchmark_baselines/<device_key>.txt`) and the only committed one was `nvidia_a100_sxm4_40gb.txt`, so on that queue `read_baseline` found nothing, and on every build the script recorded a baseline and passed. Meanwhile `.buildkite/A100_pipeline/pipeline.yml` runs `queue: clima`, which is the hardware that baseline came from, and did not run the ratchet at all.

So this moves the step rather than adding one: out of the central pipeline and into the A100 pipeline's `Benchmarks` group, `soft_fail: true` and `slurm_exclusive:` to match the other GPU lanes there. One lane, one committed baseline, and the two are the same GPU.

It also closes the path that let a ratchet run for weeks without comparing. A missing baseline for this GPU is now an error rather than a quiet record-and-pass, and so is a baseline recorded on another Julia version. That second case was invisible by construction: `write_baseline` writes `# julia: $(VERSION)`, but `read_baseline` skips comment lines, so the recorded toolchain was written and never read back. A new `baseline_julia` reads it, and since a toolchain change moves register counts, a mismatch now leaves nothing to compare against rather than something to compare across.

And it records the baseline, on the GPU and the toolchain this lane actually runs: `NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB` at Julia 1.13.3. The old `nvidia_a100_sxm4_40gb.txt` — a 40 GB card at Julia 1.12.6 — is deleted, because nothing on this queue can compare against it.

Putting the two files side by side is what shows why the mismatch was hard to see. Across the twelve measurements the new minima sit between 2.98% faster and 5.00% slower than the old ones, the widest being `all_sky_lw_Float32` at 726.2 → 762.4 ms. The 20% tolerance absorbs every one of them. So had the key ever matched, the ratchet would have read green while comparing one GPU against another at a different Julia version, and the fix is not a tighter tolerance — it is that a baseline keyed to both is the only thing a wall-time comparison can be made against.

One thing this deliberately does not do: tighten that tolerance. At 20% on wall time it catches cliffs — a register spill, a step down in occupancy, a lost early-out — and not a few percent, which is the right bound for a shared cluster and worth knowing before anyone reads a green ratchet as "no regression".

One thing the lane does not cover is worth writing down, since a ratchet is only as good as the path it measures: it does not reach the grouped solver #637 adds. `RRTMGPSolver` defaults `ngpt_groups` to `default_ngpt_groups`, but `TwoStreamLWRTE` and `TwoStreamSWRTE` default it to 1, and the high-resolution benchmarks construct those types directly — so the benchmark solves the serial g-point loop however many groups its column count would afford. Measured rather than assumed: recorded on #637's branch at this same GPU and toolchain, all twelve cases land within 0.38% of the baseline above, every ratio printing 1.00x. Covering the grouped path means passing `ngpt_groups = default_ngpt_groups(grid_params)` in the benchmark setups, or adding a case at the column counts where the default is the full 16. Either changes what is measured, so it wants its own PR and its own re-recorded baseline.

body:
From Claude:

Both two-stream solves split a column's g-point loop across the threads of a wider grid, and compute each round's gas and aerosol optics in a kernel of its own before sweeping them. Three smaller changes sit on top of that and are measured with it: a per-kernel register cap on each of the four kernels, skipping the shortwave optics where the sun is down, and interpolating the aerosol humidity once per layer instead of once per species.

## What it does

A column's `n_gpt` g-points were walked serially by one thread. They are now dealt to `ngpt_groups` threads of the same column, each accumulating its own partial flux, and one reduction kernel sums the partials.

Each launch covers all `ncol * ngpt_groups` threads, and the host walks `cld(n_gpt, ngpt_groups)` rounds of two launches -- 16 rounds in the longwave and 14 in the shortwave at the default 16 groups -- so a radiation call goes from one kernel per band to 33 and 29 counting the reduction. The launch count is not what this costs: the reduction is 1.3 ms in the longwave and 2.2 ms in the shortwave over the whole profile window below, and every percentage in this description charges the branch for it.

The mechanism is one defaulted parameter, `wcol = gcol`, threaded through the per-column bodies. `gcol` keeps addressing the atmospheric state and the boundary conditions; `wcol = gcol + (grp - 1) * ncol` addresses the wide scratch, so consecutive threads are consecutive columns of one group and the reads stay coalesced. Every existing caller and the whole CPU path are unchanged, so nothing new is specialized.

The optics split is what reaches the registers. A grouped round used to compute the optical properties and sweep them in one kernel body, which held it at 255 registers -- the cap -- and at 8 warps per multiprocessor. Splitting the body gets both halves off the cap, to 12 warps in the longwave and 16 in the shortwave, and a per-kernel `maxregs` then buys more on top. Each count below is the one its own kernel measured fastest at, over an interleaved sweep four occupancy steps deep, and the caps compose per kernel rather than as a matched pair.

| kernel | registers, uncapped | cap | warps/SM at the cap | effect of the cap alone |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| longwave optics | 156 | 96 | 20 | -11.41% |
| longwave sweeps | 140 | 72 | 28 | -8.02% |
| shortwave optics | 124 | 96 | 20 | -4.65% |
| shortwave sweeps | 117 | 64 | 32 | -5.51% |

The 128-thread block is part of the treatment. Ten block sizes were swept against one settled state, nine of them in the longwave because 512 threads exceeds that band's register budget; 128 is the fastest measured in both bands. The four kernels do not share a ceiling -- 384 reaches the longwave's best occupancy but leaves the shortwave a step down, and 256 is the mirror image -- so one block size has to be chosen against both. The thread on that comment has the table.

Two refinements the grouped structure made cheap. A night column returns from the shortwave optics without filling `op`, and the sweeps kernel zeroes that thread's slice rather than leaving whatever the workspace last held, so the reduction sums zeros to the same result; the exception is the 550 nm aerosol optical depth, which every column has whether or not the sun is up, so one nominated g-point still runs for a dark column -- 1 g-point in 224. What that can save is set by whole warps, not columns: half the columns are night at this resolution and 46.0% of the 32-lane warps are entirely so. And all eight humidity-dependent aerosol lookups -- sea salt in five size bins, sulfate, hydrophilic black carbon, hydrophilic organic carbon -- bisect the same relative humidity over the same levels, so that search runs once per `(column, layer, g-point)` instead of once per species present there. It is bit-for-bit, and worth 215.5 ms of the optics kernels on its own.

```julia
solver = RRTMGPSolver(grid_params; ...)                   # groups sized to the grid
solver = RRTMGPSolver(grid_params; ..., ngpt_groups = 1)  # the serial loop
```

Workspaces are allocated only where the grouped solve can run -- `AllSkyRadiationWithClearSkyDiagnostics`, two-stream optics, no per-band fluxes, more than one group -- so a caller keeping per-band fluxes gets the ungrouped path and none of the memory.

## Why one grid rather than one launch per group

At one thread per column the solve is 0.89 of a single resident wave, so there is nothing for concurrent launches of it to overlap with -- the first longwave implementation on this branch is that concurrent-launch version, and it measured the same saving the merged grid does. The parallelism has to come from more blocks inside each grid, which is what widening the workspaces to `ncol * ngroups` buys. The gain is waves rather than occupancy: blocks queue behind each other instead of a multiprocessor idling until the launch's slowest column is done, and columns are not equally expensive, since a column sweeps the cloudy increment only where its mask is set and a night column exits at once.

That is also why the two halves are not separable gains. At one group the solve is 24,576 resident threads however it is packaged, so shedding registers raises the ceiling and leaves nothing to put in the slots it freed. Only the grouping supplies those blocks.

## What it is worth, measured

A paired nsys profile of the coupled AMIP benchmark, 24,576 columns and 80 layers over a 120-step window, against upstream `main` at `4699d468`, re-measured on upstream main of the whole surrounding stack (ClimaCore `46b30906`, ClimaAtmos `51a998b0`, CloudMicrophysics `f7e038e2`). Every one of those is pinned to the same commit in both arms, which the measurement script derives rather than asserts, so the whole-device figure below is this branch's. Device shares are elapsed time -- the union of the kernel intervals -- not `SUM(end-start)`, which counts a moment once per resident kernel and has the opposite sign for the longwave here.

| band | baseline | this branch | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| longwave | 2,677.7 ms, one kernel at 255 registers and 8 warps/SM | 1,287.6 ms: optics 953.5, sweeps 332.9, reduction 1.3 | **-51.91%** |
| shortwave | 2,444.5 ms, one kernel at 255 registers and 8 warps/SM | 688.6 ms: optics 440.8, sweeps 245.5, reduction 2.2 | **-71.83%** |

That is 3,146 ms off a 25,498 ms device budget, and the whole budget moves with it: **-12.35%**. The resolution is not in question -- across the 21 kernels neither arm treats, the worst moved 7.9 ms, so the saving is some 400 times the drift of its own controls.

In wall clock, the paired AMIP run gives **9.405% of SYPD** -- 1.2944 to 1.4288, both arms on the same GPU -- and walltime per coupling step falls with it, 0.2538 s to 0.2299 s, which is what separates a real speedup from a coarser timestep. That is 6.9 points over the 1.869% floor from the 2 passes at this benchmark window whose arms were identical code, and wider than the 1.196-point gap between those two draws. Read it as corroboration and not as the measurement. It is one pair: the pair taken before upstream main was pulled under both arms gave 8.228%, and the two cannot be averaged, because that would average across stacks rather than repeat a measurement -- between them the baseline arm alone moved 6.79% and the mod arm 8.178%, which is upstream getting faster underneath both of them. Both nulls in the floor also have the same sign, so it is a confound that repeats rather than jitter about zero, and repeating a pair does not reduce it. The device profile is the finer instrument by a wide margin, which is why the per-kernel table is the primary evidence.

## Correctness

The grouping is **not** bit-for-bit, and that is the real cost: a 256-term `Float32` sum taken in N partials is a different summation order. What is asserted instead is that the deviation does not scale with the number of partials. The equivalence check compares the grouped solve against the serial one on live AMIP state at full resolution, at 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 16 and 24 groups -- most of which divide neither g-point count, since the ragged final stride is where a dropped or double-counted g-point would hide.

| band | n_gpt | counts not dividing it | worst relative deviation | grows with groups | cloud cover | 550 nm AOD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| longwave | 256 | 5 of 7 | 2.4e-06 | false | exact | n/a |
| shortwave | 224 | 4 of 7 | 1.0e-06 | false | exact | exact |

Fluxes are held to 1e-5 relative there; the worst observed is a quarter of that in the longwave and a tenth in the shortwave. Two things are asserted *exactly*. Cloud cover is an integer count of cloudy g-points, so the reduction either sums the groups' tallies correctly or it does not. And the 550 nm aerosol optical depth -- shortwave only, the longwave having none -- is the one quantity the split could corrupt without touching a flux: it is a read-modify-write on one per-column address that concurrent groups would interleave, so the kernel nominates the single g-point the serial loop leaves standing as its only writer.

`test/all_sky_with_aerosols_utils.jl` exercises the public API at 3 and 16 groups against the serial path in both bands, twice over, the second pass at a cloud fraction of 0.5: at a fraction of 1 every mask entry is true and the McICA key is never consulted, so a key drawn for `wcol` where `gcol` was meant would leave both arms identical. It also builds the one-group workspaces directly, since `RRTMGPSolver` refuses a one-group grouped path, and asserts the net flux, the clear-sky flux and the cover **exactly** against the serial solve, plus the direct beam and both aerosol optical depth fields in the shortwave -- `== 0.0`, not a tolerance, because at one group nothing is reassociated and anything less than exact is a bug. It replaced an earlier test comparing two grouped variants against each other, which could not see a bug in the code they shared; both bugs below are exactly that.

The McICA draw is keyed on `(key, gcol, igpt)` and only the destination buffer is indexed by `wcol`, so which group computes a g-point's mask cannot change which mask that g-point gets.

## Two bugs, and why the GitHub checks could not have found them

The grouped path lives entirely in `ext/RRTMGPCUDAExt`, and this repo's GitHub Actions matrix is CPU-only. Every GitHub-hosted job was green, `downstream ClimaCoupler.jl` included, while the grouped path **had never compiled**:

- `_accumulate_fluxes!` still required `flux_acc::FluxLW` / `::FluxSW` after the accumulators became NamedTuples of views, so the grouped kernels died at compile with `InvalidIRError: unsupported call to jl_f_throw_methoderror`.
- The reduction read accumulator plane 4 of a 3-plane array under `@inbounds`, summing the shortwave direct beam from past the end of the array. The reduce kernels now read the accumulators through their named views, so a plane layout is unreferenceable from a kernel.

The second was unreachable while the first stood, which is why no test could have caught it: nothing ever got far enough to produce a wrong number. Buildkite, which does have a GPU, is green on the current head (build #1521); the one red check is `codecov/patch`, on CUDA-extension lines its runner cannot execute.

## Defaults and what it costs

`default_ngpt_groups(grid_params)` asks for enough groups to reach `TARGET_GPT_GROUP_COLUMNS` wide columns, capped at `MAX_NGPT_GROUPS = 16` and at what a sixteenth of the device's own memory affords on the grid's level count and float type. A column count that already fills the device gets one group, and so does a CPU, whose driver ignores the workspaces. Both gates matter: the count rises as columns fall, so an ungated default would give the smallest runs the widest workspaces, and neither `nlev` nor the float type is in the column target, so the byte bound is what catches a deep grid or a `Float64` one. That bound is a share of **total** device memory rather than of what is free, deliberately: the group count fixes the order a column's g-points are summed, so pricing it against free memory would make the fluxes depend on what the host had already allocated when the solver was built. On the 80 GiB A100 this runs on it reads 4.95 GiB against 227 MB a group at the benchmark's shape, so it is inert there and the default is the full 16; it first binds at 118 layers, and at `Float64` it allows 11 groups rather than 16.

16 is a measurement rather than the first count that worked. The longwave solve was swept over 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 groups in one process against one settled state, before the register caps landed: most of the gain is in by 8 groups, which reach 92% of the best saving at half the default's memory. Raising the cap to 32 is worth another 1.9 points of that solve for twice the workspace, and 64 is slower than 32 -- the curve turns over inside the sweep rather than running to the endpoint. Both of those are far under the noise floor of the coupled model, so neither could be confirmed by running it.

The cost at the default is 1.575 GiB in the longwave and 1.812 GiB in the shortwave, counted rather than measured: 13 planes of the grid's float type per wide column per level in the longwave and 15 in the shortwave, plus a byte of cloud mask, which is what `gpt_group_bytes` sums and what the bound above is checked against. It agrees with the device free-memory delta taken across construction to the three figures that was reported at, 1.58 and 1.81 GiB, and `test/gpt_group_workspaces.jl` holds the count to the arrays the constructors actually allocate, so a field added to any of them cannot leave it silently low. Together that is 4.3% of the device it runs on, and a smaller card does not pay a larger share, because the bound scales with the card: a 40 GiB A100 takes 11 groups at the benchmark's shape and a 16 GiB P100 four. `NEWS.md` leads with the result change, since the default is above one group on a GPU: fluxes differ from a serial solve by about 1e-6 relative, the clear-sky half of a both-skies solve no longer equals a standalone clear-sky solve exactly, and the cover stays exact. Pass `ngpt_groups = 1` where bit-for-bit agreement with the serial order is required.

## Outstanding

Review feedback not yet applied, all structural rather than numerical: unifying `LWGptGroups` and `SWGptGroups` into one struct with aliases, merging the two sweeps kernels and the two reductions now that their bodies have converged, deleting a dead `FT = eltype(acc.flux_up)` in both sweeps kernels, and spelling `FT(0)` as `zero(FT)` in the two reductions. The first two move register counts, so they want one re-run of the equivalence check and the register readback, and the block-size sweep is pinned to the current counts for the same reason.

Two commits are kept deliberately rather than squashed: the first longwave implementation is the concurrent-launch one and the second replaces it, and commits in the measurement repository point their submodule pointer at the first, so squashing would orphan them.
